account:
Today the unusual thing is persistent talk about a bridge or port change, apparently discussed at the bakery without any clear proposal reaching my office. Townsfolk repeated reports naming the baker, innkeeper, builder, freight organiser and neighbour in different combinations. These are secondhand reports, not proof that all those people are organising something. I tried to ask the baker directly, but the baker left without hearing my question. I have now arrived for my scheduled fifteen-hundred tea at the neighbour's cottage and asked for firsthand details; I have not yet received an answer. It might concern transport or river access, given the bridge and port references, but I do not yet know its purpose or whether any actual change is planned.

The ten-o'clock mill grain inspection was also incomplete: nobody identified a responsible mill contact, and the secretary could not locate the manager. I saw 68 hay bales at the mill stall, priced at two emeralds each, but did not verify grain quality or accounts. This is an unresolved piece of town business, not evidence that it is connected with the rumours. No council letters reached the secretary for our thirteen-hundred appointment. The secretary said they would record that, seek a mill contact through the baker or freight organiser, and invite the actual bridge or port proposers to my office tomorrow morning. My subsequent dictated mill letter went unheard, so I cannot assume it will be prepared.

The builder has reported the hall lanterns in good order, and an eighteen-hundred great hall lighting inspection remains on my schedule, alongside my sixteen-thirty office appointment. I have no direct evidence of wrongdoing or a hidden purpose; I chiefly notice that discussion is circulating among townspeople while I still lack a clear firsthand explanation.
